Rose George is a British journalist and author. She has been a postwar correspondent, a writer of reportage, and a regular book reviewer. She has written four non-fiction books. "A Life Removed, The Big Necessity: The Unmentionable World of Human Waste and Why it Matters"; "Deep Sea and Foreign Going: Inside Shipping, the Invisible Industry the Brings you 90% of Everything"; "Nine Pints: A Journey Through the Money, Medicine, and Mysteries of Blood" and "Every Last Fish: A Deep Dive into the World of Fishes and Fishing."

These colonists insisted that Africans hadn't built Great Zimbabwe, instead claiming it arose from the Phoenicians, a people originally from the Mediterranean; they used that inaccuracy to justify taking all the artifacts to England, according to the documentary. The Society of Collision Repair Specialists (SCRS) has shared details about the third and final session of its 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit, which will wrap up an afternoon program focused on vehicle safety, from national objectives to vehicle engineering and into the collision repair process.

“Preserving the Safety System: Sensors, Calibration and Repairability” will take place Thursday, Nov. 5, from 3:30–4:30 p.m. during the SEMA Show in Las Vegas, featuring ADAS systems and service engineering experts from General Motors, Ford Motor Co., and Rivian.
SCRS says the session will answer for repairers what it takes to preserve and restore the ADAS safety capabilities engineered into the vehicle after collisions.

“Cameras, radar, and other sensing technologies are fundamentally changing what vehicles can understand about the environment around them,” an SCRS press release states. “These systems can identify objects, measure distance and velocity, recognize roadway conditions, and combine information from multiple sensors to support increasingly sophisticated vehicle decisions. That capability also introduces extraordinary precision into the collision repair process.”

The third OEM Summit session will bring together the GM, Ford, and Rivian engineers who are responsible for sensing systems, vehicle performance, calibration strategies, and service engineering so they can discuss what today’s sensors can do, what can affect their performance, and how automakers translate engineering requirements into repair procedures and field instructions.

- Steven Vance, principal hardware engineer, engineering technical leader, and ADAS sensors and sensing systems at GM — among his responsibilities are sensor capabilities and requirements that affect repair, including sensor modalities and strengths, the importance of sensor alignment, and the potential influence of aftermarket accessories on sensing performance.

- Chad Zagorski, principal systems engineer and ADAS at GM — develops new ADAS technologies and improves existing systems, focusing on enhancing ADAS performance across GM’s vehicle lineup. His work combines engineering and product development with industry collaboration on standards and test-method development.

- Brian Perkins, body and damageability commodity manager of design for service at Ford — leads Ford’s collision and damageability team and oversees the Paint and Body Technology Center. His team represents collision repair technicians within Ford’s global organization by testing and validating repair tools and procedures. SCRS says this work ensures that technicians have the information necessary to properly repair Ford vehicles, including increasingly important ADAS documentation.

- Ryan Davenport, service engineering, propulsion and electronics senior manager at Rivian — oversees service program launches, ADAS and propulsion diagnostics, and incident resolution. His work includes troubleshooting complex vehicle systems, ensuring Rivian’s electric vehicles meet service and safety requirements, and improving the technician and customer experience.

SCRS says the panelists will explore how sensors are designed to operate and how variables introduced by a collision or repair, such as sensor position, mounting locations, structural dimensions, wheel alignment, ride height, replacement glass, body materials, and other seemingly small changes, can affect what a vehicle’s sensing systems perceive.
The discussion, moderated by Database Enhancement Gateway (DEG) Administrator Danny Gredinberg, will also take attendees behind the development of collision repair information to cover:
- How engineering requirements become service procedures;
- How calibration strategies are established and tested; and
- What a successful calibration actually verifies about system performance.

“Those questions grow increasingly significant as crash avoidance and mitigation technologies play a larger role in vehicle safety,” the release states. “The session will ultimately confront a question with direct implications for every business repairing modern vehicles: what must a collision repair facility do to confidently determine that a vehicle’s safety systems have been restored to the performance its manufacturer intended?”

SCRS says together, the three 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit sessions are designed to tell a connected story about vehicle safety: “What safety outcomes is the nation trying to achieve? How are those outcomes engineered into the vehicle? And after a collision, how do we preserve them?”

For collision repair professionals working on modern vehicles, SCRS encourages attendees to participate in the entire series rather than viewing the sessions independently. To register for the entire summit, click here.

The afternoon begins with “The National Safety Objective: Safer Vehicles, Safer Roads,” featuring National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) Deputy Administrator Lee White, who will examine federal vehicle and roadway safety priorities.

The second session, “Engineering the Safety Benefit: From Requirement to Real-World Performance,” features safety and ADAS engineering leaders from General Motors, who will explore how automakers translate safety objectives into vehicle technologies. It will also cover how they establish performance requirements and evaluate whether those technologies produce measurable safety benefits in the real world.

Panelists will include Michael Carpenter, General Motors Active Safety and Global Vehicle Performance owner; Jameson Collins, General Motors Active Safety and staff product manager; and Jeremy Nelson, Ford Motor Co. ADAS application systems engineer.
The 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit is part of SCRS’ Repairer Driven Education (RDE) program at the SEMA Show, which includes several classes, the IDEAS Collide Showcase, and more.

An SCRS RDE Full Series Pass provides access to Tuesday and Wednesday RDE sessions, IDEAS Collide, the OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit, and the SCRS Afterparty. To register for the full series pass, click here.
For additional information about SCRS and Repairer Driven Education, visit scrs.com/rde.

FORVIA announced the appointment of Olivier Lefebvre as head of the JIKA (Japan, India, Korea and ASEAN) region, effective immediately. Lefebvre also serves as chief operating officer and group executive vice president. The company said his appointment strengthens FORVIA’s operational governance and execution capabilities across one of the group’s key geographic areas.
FORVIA Expands Lefebvre’s Leadership Responsibilities

Lefebvre has experience transforming industrial operations and leading complex global projects. He joined the group in 1995 and has held several senior leadership roles across South America and Europe. Most recently, he led FORVIA’s Clean Mobility business group.
As chief operating officer, he oversees operational excellence across the group. His responsibilities include operations, total customer satisfaction and quality, and purchasing.

The appointment reflects FORVIA’s focus on regional leadership, customer relationships and operational excellence. It also supports the execution of strategic priorities through coordination with regional leadership teams.
Lefebvre succeeds Shoji Akiyama, who has decided to pursue opportunities outside the group. FORVIA thanked Akiyama for his contributions and leadership during his tenure.

“The JIKA region is an important contributor to FORVIA’s global operations and customer relationships. By expanding Olivier’s responsibilities, we are strengthening the connection between regional execution and the Group’s operational leadership, with a continued focus on performance, agility and customer support,” said Martin Fischer, chief executive officer of FORVIA. “This appointment will also help accelerate our local-for-local strategy, ensuring that we remain close to our customers and continue developing solutions tailored to the specific needs of each market.”

“I am honored to take on the leadership of the JIKA region, alongside my current responsibilities,” said Lefebvre. “JIKA is a strategic region for FORVIA, supported by talented teams, strong customer relationships and significant growth opportunities. Together, we will continue to focus on operational excellence, customer satisfaction and the successful execution of our priorities, while further strengthening FORVIA’s position across the region.”

Klipboard, an industry-specific business software company, is marking its 50th anniversary. October 2026 marks five decades of supporting businesses with industry-specific software and expertise. The company has helped businesses adapt, grow and make the most of changing technology.

Founded in 1976 as Kerridge Computer Company, the business has changed significantly over the past half-century. The company began by developing software for niche industries in the U.K. Today, Klipboard provides industry-specific business management technology to 55,000 customers across automotive, distribution, rental and field service.
Klipboard Adapts to Technological Changes

The milestone comes as the pace of technological change continues to accelerate. Over the past 50 years, Klipboard has helped businesses navigate the arrival of personal computing and graphical user interfaces. Other developments include the internet, cloud computing and mobile technology, alongside periods of significant economic and industry change.

Today, developments in artificial intelligence, data and automation are creating another major shift in business operations and decision-making. Throughout these changes, Klipboard said it has continued to evolve its technology around the industries and businesses it serves.
Today, Klipboard operates across 30 global offices. The company combines international scale with industry expertise developed through decades of working closely with customers.

“50 years is a remarkable milestone, and one that gives us an opportunity to reflect on just how much has changed,” said Ian Bendelow, CEO of Klipboard. “Since Klipboard began its journey, we’ve seen the arrival of the internet, mobile phones, cloud computing, social media and now artificial intelligence. We’ve also lived through economic booms, recessions, global crises and enormous changes within the industries our customers operate in.”

“I’m incredibly proud of what we’ve built together and grateful to every customer, partner and employee who has been part of that journey. But while 50 years gives us plenty to celebrate, what excites me most is what comes next.”
From Industry Software to Connected Business Technology

Klipboard said its development over five decades reflects the changing role technology plays within the businesses it supports. Early business systems helped companies manage everyday processes. Today, technology plays a fundamental role in managing inventory, sales, customers, assets, finance and operations. It also helps organizations manage the information behind their business decisions.

Klipboard has evolved alongside these requirements. The company develops and integrates industry-specific enterprise resource planning (ERP) and business management solutions around customers’ operations. This evolution continues today.

Alongside its core business management platforms, Klipboard is investing in cloud technology, connected applications, embedded payments and data intelligence. The company also is investing in solutions with native or embedded artificial intelligence (AI). These technologies aim to reduce manual work, improve visibility and support better-informed decisions.

The company recently introduced Klipboard Intelligence, which combines industry-specific operational data, industry expertise and advanced analytics. The technology aims to help businesses understand changing conditions and identify areas requiring action.

Klipboard plans to mark its 50th anniversary throughout the year by recognizing customers, employees, partnerships and innovations that shaped the business. A new timeline charts milestones from 1976 to today. It covers the company’s early years, initial software developments, international expansion and successive generations of technology. The company also intends to use the anniversary to highlight its future direction.

“The technology will continue to change, just as it has throughout our first 50 years. Our job is to understand what those changes mean for our customers and turn them into something genuinely useful,” Bendelow added. “We’ve achieved a huge amount together in our first 50 years. Now we can build on that experience and help our customers navigate whatever comes next.”

Ranger, a division of BendPak, introduced the next-generation DST30PX wheel balancer as part of its DST Series. As shops face an influx of larger OEM wheel assemblies and heavy aftermarket truck tires, older balancing platforms can struggle. These challenges can slow the balancing process.
The Ranger DST30PX Professional Wheel Balancer accommodates oversized wheels through a new hood design, larger shaft and redesigned structural chassis.
Wheel Balancer Accommodates Oversized Assemblies

According to Ranger, the new hood accommodates a wider range of tire shapes and sizes, including oversized off-road and fleet tires. Its design reduces the need for repositioning. The open-side design allows technicians to mount wider tires, aggressive offsets and bulky sidewalls more easily. This reduces setup time and helps operators position wheel assemblies up to 43 inches in diameter.

Ranger also reinforced the machine’s chassis and hood assembly to handle the added mass of larger assemblies. The reinforcement reduces flexing, alignment issues and excess vibration. The additional rigidity helps maintain consistent measurements during operation. The 40 mm shaft increases stiffness and accuracy for heavier wheels while supporting standard cones and accessories.

“The Ranger DST30PX represents a fundamental shift in how modern shops handle today’s radically heavier, oversized wheel configurations,” says Sean Price, director of product development for BendPak Inc. “By optimizing the physical layout and integrating a high-precision sensor array, we ensure technicians can mount, spin, and perfectly balance oversized assemblies without a single second of wasted motion — turning massive wheel packages into a rapid, routine six-second floor-to-floor operation.”
Encoder Supports Accurate Weight Placement
Ranger added that the DST30PX features a large, 64-tooth magnetic transducer encoder that uses precision-cut square teeth. The encoder converts rotary position into a digital electronic signal.
This technology helps the machine achieve accurate profile readings and top-dead-center positioning for precise wheel weight placement.

The additional encoder resolution supports balancing applications requiring smaller weight adjustments and greater placement accuracy. These applications include performance wheels and larger tires, where customers may notice even minor vibration issues.
The DST30PX streamlines repetitive wheel service by reducing unnecessary motion.

Simple wheel data entry, precise rolling weight readings and automatic braking help technicians balance wheels efficiently. Manual or automatic hood-start operation and a rapid cycle time also help reduce errors and guesswork.
The quick-release hub nut, side-position brake, top-dead-center weight indicator and tiered placement indicators accelerate setup and correction.

Onboard storage includes a high-volume top tray, side cone pegs and a side shelf. The shelf accommodates Ranger Quick-Peel adhesive tape weight rolls. These features help technicians organize their work areas during busy periods.
Other key features of the Ranger DST30PX Professional Wheel Balancer include:
- 145-pound capacity, 30-inch wheel diameter range and maximum tire diameter of 43 inches
- Low-rpm balancing operation and six-second cycle time
- Dynamic, static and performance alloy settings
- 16-bit processor and multidirectional quartz piezoelectric sensors that detect imbalance across multiple force directions
- Automatic braking and self-calibration function
Safety Certification and Included Accessories

The Ranger DST30PX Professional Wheel Balancer offers shops a measuring system for modern wheels without requiring a larger machine. The machine carries ETL certification for applicable UL and CSA safety standards in the United States and Canada.

Like other Ranger balancers, the DST30PX includes a starter kit of adhesive and clip-on steel wheel weights. Ranger also offers its Ranger Select setup and training program. Additional information is available on the Ranger DST30PX product page or by calling 800-253-2363.

The fifth-generation Ram 2500 places substantial demands on its brakes. Many of these trucks carry heavy payloads, tow trailers or operate in fleets, so a successful brake job requires a complete-system inspection and parts that match the platform’s thermal and mechanical demands.

This Brake Job covers the 2019-present fifth-generation Ram 2500, not the Ram 1500. The 2500 uses heavy-duty components and platform-specific procedures. Confirm the model year, engine, axle and options before ordering parts or applying specifications.
The Ram 2500 has four-wheel vented discs and dual-piston sliding calipers. Separate parking-brake shoes act against a drum surface inside each rear rotor hat.

Booster configuration depends on the engine. The 6.4L Hemi uses a dual-diaphragm vacuum booster and an electric vacuum pump near the left front of the engine to supplement engine vacuum. The PCM commands the pump based on operating inputs. The 6.7L diesel uses Hydro-Boost, supplied by the power-steering pump, with an accumulator providing limited reserve assist if pump pressure is lost.

When it’s practical, begin the process with a road test and note pedal travel, assist, pull, vibration and noise under normal braking. Confirm the complaint before disassembly; a vibration blamed on the front brakes may originate at the rear, and an assist complaint may come from the vacuum or power-steering circuit rather than the foundation brakes.

Clean around the master-cylinder cap and verify that the fluid is at the MAX mark. On a diesel vehicle, you should also inspect the power-steering fluid level, hoses and lines, because Hydro-Boost depends on that circuit. Low fluid, leaks, restrictions or weak pump output can create assist complaints. On gasoline models, inspect booster vacuum plumbing and electric-pump operation.

Compare inner and outer pad wear and both sides of each axle. Uneven wear can reveal seized hardware, binding pads, piston trouble or slide problems. Replace pads as an axle set if usable lining at the thinnest point is 1 mm (0.04 inch) or less. Inspect boots, pistons, slides, hoses and bleeders for damage, leakage and corrosion.

Be sure to measure the rotors. Minimum thickness is 37.4 mm (1.47 inches) front and 32.4 mm (1.28 inches) rear. Maximum runout is 0.020 mm (0.0008 inch); maximum loose-rotor thickness variation is 0.008 mm (0.00031 inch). You should also inspect the internal parking-brake surface; maximum drum diameter is 207.2 mm (8.157 inches).

Support the caliper and adapter; never let the hose carry their weight. Clean the pad lands and hub face without removing base metal. Install new anti-rattle clips, verify free pad movement and make sure both pistons retract smoothly. Because the rotor fits over the hub studs, hub cleanliness and uniform wheel-fastener torque are critical to controlling installed runout.

Rear service adds the parking-brake assembly. A rotor that will not release may be hanging on the shoes, so release the pedal and back off the star wheel if necessary. With the rotor off, inspect the shoes, springs, adjuster, cable action and drum surface. Clean the hub and bracket, verify piston and slide movement, and install new hardware and sealing washers as required.
Always replace caliper hardware; old clips can restrict pad movement and cause uneven wear.

Use fresh fluid meeting SAE J1703-F and DOT 3 standards. Bleed in this order: right rear, left rear, right front and left front, keeping the reservoir full. For pressure bleeding, use the correct adapter; 15-20 PSI is generally sufficient, depending on equipment limits.

If air entered the HCU, perform a base bleed, use a capable scan tool’s ABS Miscellaneous menu to run the HCU bleed routine, then bleed the base system again. Set the fluid level and verify a firm pedal.

Hydro-Boost is generally self- bleeding. Fill the power-steering reservoir, disable the engine and crank it for several seconds, then recheck the level. Re-enable and start the engine, slowly turn lock to lock twice, shut it off and discharge the accumulator with five pedal applications. Restart, repeat two slow lock-to-lock cycles, shut down and correct the level. If the fluid foams, let it dissipate before repeating the final cycles.

Adjust the shoes before cable tension. With the pedal fully released and the front cable slackened at the frame-rail adjuster, turn each star wheel through the backing-plate hole until slight drag is felt, then back it off until drag disappears. Adjust both sides equally.

Cable-tensioner adjustment is normally required only after replacement or disconnection. After verifying cable movement and shoe adjustment, fully apply the pedal. Mark the non-threaded tensioner rod 1/4 inch from the tensioner edge and tighten the nut until the mark disappears. Release the pedal, confirm both wheels rotate freely, verify that the brake holds and road-test the truck.
DRiV announced the expansion of its Wagner brake caliper portfolio with the addition of 547 new SKUs, bringing the lineup to approximately 1,100 SKUs.
According to DRiV, the expanded coverage includes the 2015 Nissan Altima and 2013 Hyundai Sonata. Wagner says its calipers are 100% new units, and the program requires no core charge or core return.

“Wagner continues to invest in the categories and coverage areas that matter most to aftermarket customers,” said Joseph Saoud, vice president and general manager for the U.S. and Canada at DRiV. “With 547 new caliper SKUs, we are expanding availability across high-volume vehicle applications while giving customers a 100% new caliper option that helps simplify the repair and replacement process.”

Circle track racing represents one of the most technically demanding environments for an internal combustion engine. Whether the surface is dirt or asphalt, these engines must survive sustained high rpm, extreme lateral g-forces and the unpredictable conditions that develop over the course of a race night. Unlike drag racing engines built for seconds of peak output, circle track powerplants must deliver broad, controllable power for hundreds of laps while maintaining durability.

That balance between power, drivability and longevity defines successful circle track engine development. According to Luke Wilson of 4 Piston Racing and Jack Cornett of Cornett Racing Engines, designing an engine for this environment requires a different mindset than nearly any other racing discipline. The two builders gave us their perspectives on engines for this application.

One of the defining characteristics of a competitive circle track engine is how usable its power is throughout the race. Conditions change constantly during an event, particularly on dirt tracks where the racing surface evolves lap after lap.

Early in the evening, dirt tracks may be heavy and fast, rewarding engines that produce strong high-rpm horsepower. But as the racing surface changes and slicks off, the characteristics required from the engine can shift dramatically.

“In qualifying and early heat races, the tracks can be heavy, so big, high-rpm power can be the fastest thing out there,” Wilson explains. “If there are yellow flags and restart after restart, a good, strong, low-end grunt engine may work you through to the front.”
Later in the night, drivers may be forced to maintain speed with minimal throttle input as traction becomes scarce.

“As the track slicks off in the longer races, the driver has to have the ability to run around the track fast at as little as 40% throttle…then be able to dig into their bank of power as they find places in the dirt that will hold more,” Wilson says.
This constantly changing environment means builders rarely chase peak dyno numbers alone. Instead, they focus on creating an engine with a broad, controllable powerband.

“The real balance is in making sure an engine is responsive on a restart, strong through the middle and can carry rpm to your mandated rpm,” Wilson says. “The engine has to be smooth and controllable by the driver, who is sitting in a strange position and bouncing all over the place.”

While power delivery is critical, durability is equally important. Circle track engines spend extended periods operating at extremely high rpm, which creates unique challenges for internal components.

“In circle track racing, the engine has to be built with endurance and longevity in mind,” Cornett says. “It’s completely opposite of drag racing or tractor pulling. Our engines must go 600 miles at 9,000 rpm.”

Sustained operation at these speeds places enormous stress on the rotating assembly and valvetrain components. Builders must carefully balance lightweight choices for acceleration with materials capable of surviving long-term fatigue.
“Selecting bottom end components is a balancing act,” Cornett explains. “You want the lightest components possible for acceleration, but they have to be durable enough to last thousands of miles.”
This philosophy extends to the entire engine package, from connecting rods and pistons to camshaft profiles and valvetrain components.

“Compromises have to be made in an endurance application with camshaft profiles and valvetrain components, compression ratio and ignition timing, plus carb jetting,” Cornett says. “All these factor heavily into the longevity of the engine.”

One of the most critical systems in a circle track engine is lubrication. Sustained lateral forces during cornering can starve engines of oil if the system is not designed specifically for oval racing.
“The oiling system in our engines has to be dry sump only,” Cornett says. “There is no way the engine can survive without it.”

Dry sump systems allow builders to maintain a stable oil supply while also managing oil control within the engine. Specialized oil pans and tanks are engineered specifically for left-turn racing and the lateral g-forces the engines and cars experience.

“Good, clean, non-aerated oil is critical to longevity,” Wilson says. “These engines typically have good dry sump systems that will work well on these short runs. Controlling where that oil goes and how clean the oil supply is gives you a longer-lasting engine.”
Because engine architectures vary widely across circle track classes, oil pressure requirements can differ significantly as well.

“There are very short-stroke engines with big pins on both ends, and there are smaller-displacement, small-bore, large-stroke engines – like what we build – that really require a different type of oil pressure and rebuild schedule,” Wilson notes.

Temperature management is another critical factor in circle track engine performance and reliability. Unlike many drag racing engines that run relatively cool, circle track engines often operate at significantly higher temperatures for extended periods.

“In dirt midget racing, engines are preheated to 190 degrees F with diesel or electric units and then they go push off and run,” Wilson explains. “They never have a problem having temperature in them. In fact, many of them are run too hot.”
Limited cooling capacity and the challenges of racing on dirt often contribute to high operating temperatures.

“They have small radiators with no fans, and they can get packed with dirt,” Wilson says. “Teams often come off the track with engines that have more temperature in them than the engine builders want to see.”
Cornett notes that maintaining proper operating temperatures is essential for engine survival.

“Heat management is very important and it becomes critical on dirt due to the surface you are racing on,” Cornett says. “We want to keep the water temp in the 200-240 degree F range and the oil temp in the 220-260 degree F range.”
Fuel tuning is sometimes used as an additional method of temperature control. “They often are running rich lambda outside of optimal to help keep the engines cool,” Wilson says.
Clearances, Bearings and Ring Strategies
While circle track engines operate in extreme conditions, many builders rely on proven fundamentals when it comes to internal clearances.
“There is no black magic here,” Wilson says. “Run your bearing clearance that you would normally run for your engine you are building and the oil you are running.”
For the engines built at 4 Piston Racing, that typically means clearances between .0018” and .0022”. However, Wilson notes that he’s seen other run larger clearances without engine issues as well.

Ring gap selection follows a similar philosophy. Run the ring gaps that your piston design engineer determined for your piston. “Adjust as you analyze your engines when they come back for service,” Wilson says.
One factor builders must monitor carefully is the presence of excess fuel in the ring lands, particularly when running methanol with constant-flow fuel systems.

“I have observed many times where teams run overly rich on these constant flow systems and will have a lot of unburned methanol sitting in the ring lands,” Wilson says. “There is power and longevity in having this properly managed.”
Cornett notes that ring gap strategies continue to evolve as piston and ring designs become thinner, narrower and more efficient.
As with most forms of motorsport, rulebooks play a major role in shaping circle track engine architecture.
“Rules dictate everything we do,” Wilson admits. “But this type of racing can often leave you a lot of flexibility in individual internal decisions.”
Builders typically maximize displacement and rpm within the limits set by sanctioning bodies, but internal design decisions still allow room for innovation.
“If you took the top five engines out there, you’d see some significant differences in how they are built because the engine architecture is so different,” Wilson says.
In some classes, that freedom is one of the reasons circle track racing remains attractive to engine builders.

“There is a lot of parity in midget engines,” Wilson says. “It is about as blank sheet as you can get for wanting to build something you can call yours. Many other types of racing have gone too far on requiring a spec engine.”

Cornett echoes that sentiment from the perspective of dirt late model racing, saying, “Rules are obviously always a big concern on how to build your engine. Luckily, in dirt late model racing, there aren’t many rules.”

Despite careful engineering, circle track engines face numerous potential failure points based on engine type as each has a different Achillies heel. According to Cornett, two issues appear more frequently than others.

“The two most common failures in circle track racing are bearing failure and overheating,” he says. “I think most bearing failures are caused by not properly warming up the oil temp before you race. Overheating issues are usually caused by racing on dirt.”
Wilson notes that valvetrain components and timing drive systems can also be vulnerable.

“Engines can see valvetrain and rod bearing issues because of how the racers beat them on the limiter repeatedly,” he says. “Crashes can create additional risks. The most common failure is in the timing drive system when a car is turned backwards, flipped, or crashed in a bad way.”
Ignition system limitations can also contribute to engine stress in some racing classes.

“We have observed repeatedly where we are asking for 25 degrees of timing and will see an engine walk around as much as 10 degrees in either direction,” Wilson explains. “This is really hard on engines and easily resolved by putting a modern motorsports grade ignition system on the engine.”

Because circle track engines operate under extreme conditions, regular service and inspection are essential for maintaining performance and reliability. Cornett Racing Engines typically bases rebuild intervals on total laps run.
“Based on our experience, we have developed a lap strategy to know when to rebuild the engine,” Cornett says. “The customer keeps up with how many laps he races.”
Most engines are serviced after roughly 1,200 to 1,500 laps, which equates to approximately 600 to 750 miles of racing.
Wilson notes that service intervals can vary widely depending on how teams operate their equipment.

“I have the same engine that I’m confident that team A can run for 25 shows and then bring it for service,” he says. “I have the same engine with team B and I have them bring it back after 10 shows, sometimes in a box and not on a stand.”
Driver behavior, maintenance practices and tuning decisions all influence how long an engine survives between rebuilds.
“Some teams beat the hell out of stuff and aren’t kind to their engines,” Wilson admits. “You have to handle each team on a case-by-case basis and then develop a plan going forward.”
The Future of Circle Track Engine Technology

Even with decades of development behind them, circle track engines continue to evolve. Wilson believes that modern electronics and fuel systems could significantly improve reliability and performance in some classes.

“Midget racing specifically needs to allow some modern electronics and fueling,” he says. “Many series still rely on constant-flow fuel injection systems, which came about in the 1940s. The reality is the guys who know it well and tune it well are aging out.”

Wilson has personally tested modern electronic fuel injection systems against traditional mechanical setups. The results demonstrated that modern systems can be competitive while offering improved tuning efficiency.

“With a highly experienced constant flow pro we spent more than six hours tuning that engine,” Wilson recalls. “I swapped the injection over to my EFI, hooked up my ECU and swung a dyno pull. It cleared what we achieved on the first pull.”
Within a handful of pulls, the EFI system produced measurable gains.
“After six dyno pulls we had a smoother power curve, more responsive power and more peak power by 8–10 horsepower on a 400-hp engine,” Wilson says.
Despite the results, many teams remain loyal to traditional systems – a reminder that racing technology often evolves as much through culture as engineering.

For engine builders, circle track racing offers a unique challenge. The engines must deliver high power, survive extreme conditions and adapt to constantly changing track surfaces – all while operating within rulebooks that vary widely from one class to another. That complexity is exactly what keeps builders engaged.
“This always changing dynamic is what makes the engines in this racing so much fun to work with,” Wilson says.

As both Wilson and Cornett emphasize, success in circle track racing ultimately comes down to balancing engineering precision with real-world durability – building engines that can not only make power, but keep making it lap after lap.

In this episode of Counter Culture, Pat Burrow, technical director at International Lubricants, discusses the causes of torque converter shudder. He also explains the importance of transmission fluid and how friction modifiers can help technicians diagnose and address the problem.
Counter Culture is presented by Counterman magazine.
China has proposed a new draft rule to set standards for remanufactured auto parts, according to multiple media sources.
Business Today Malaysia reports the proposal sets requirements for sourcing used components, product quality, traceability, and market supervision.
The draft rules focus on collecting, processing, labeling, and selling parts recovered from end-of-life vehicles, according to the article.
“They aim to ensure remanufactured components meet or exceed the quality of equivalent new products,” the article states.
Bloomberg reports that the proposal would provide product traceability and more oversight of the remanufacturing market.
Engines, steering systems, transmissions, front and rear axles, and vehicle frames are all parts that could be regulated, Business Today adds.

“Remanufacturers would be required to obtain these components through qualified vehicle dismantlers and ensure the recovered parts correspond to the products they intend to remanufacture,” Business Today states.
The proposal would prohibit the remanufacturing of exhaust after-treatment devices.

On Thursday, Oct. 15, the National Distracted Driving Coalition (NDDC) will host “Technology Transforming Transportation: Innovation to Eliminate Distracted Driving”, a national event highlighting how artificial intelligence (AI), vehicle safety systems, driver attention technology, telematics and connected roadway technologies can help address distracted driving and other major road safety challenges. The event will be livestreamed free to the public 8:30-10 a.m. and 1:30-4:30 p.m. EST.

The event at the IIHS-HLDI Vehicle Research Center brings together federal transportation leaders, researchers, automakers, technology companies, law enforcement and advocates to examine how emerging and existing technologies can help prevent crashes.
- Opening keynote – 8:50 a.m. EST: Jonathan Morrison, administrator, National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA)
- Closing keynote and call to action – 4:15 p.m. EST: Thomas Chapman, board member, National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB)
- Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS)
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)
- Virginia Tech Transportation Institute

Sessions will explore how better data can identify risk before a crash, how AI and vehicle systems can support driver attention, how technology can help officers detect distracted driving and how advanced driver-assistance systems can improve safety while keeping drivers engaged.
Live Crash Test and Technology Demonstrations
Live IIHS Crash Test & Research Facility Tour
10:30 a.m.-12 p.m. EST: Attendees will witness a live vehicle crash test at the IIHS-HLDI Vehicle Research Center and get a behind-the-scenes look at vehicle safety testing and evaluation.
12-1:30 p.m. EST: A hands-on opportunity to experience technologies designed to identify risk, support drivers and improve roadway safety.
Participating technology demonstration partners include: CMT.AI; Seeing Machines; CARIAD; Mazda; Subaru; HAAS Alert; Acusensus; BusPatrol; and Virginia Tech Transportation Institute.

Demonstrations include technology involving driver attention and fatigue detection, AI-powered roadway intelligence, in-vehicle hazard warnings, vehicle safety systems, technology-assisted enforcement and other approaches.
Both the crash test and technology demonstrations are in-person only.

Although distracted driving is the focus, many of these technologies also have potential applications for speeding, impairment, seat belt use and other roadway risks. The event is intended to encourage collaboration across transportation safety disciplines and help consumers, policymakers and communities understand the solutions available today. It coincides with National Do Not Disturb While Driving Day.

The 15th annual MSO Symposium Nov. 2 at Rio Hotel & Casino will host three senior-level executive panel discussions featuring speakers from Allstate, RB Global, Boyd Group, Caliber, Classic Collision and Crash Champions, among others.

As claim frequency declines and total loss rates continue to rise, collision repair organizations are rethinking how they drive growth. Representatives from Certified Collision Group, CollisionRight, Puget Collision and Quality Collision Group will come to the stage for a look at adaptation strategies in “Navigating Revenue” and “Growth Amid a Changing Market.”

Following the event’s PPG-sponsored networking luncheon, Jim Kessler, CEO of RB Global, Mario Rizzo, COO and APD at Allstate, and Tim Welsh, president of CCC Intelligent Solutions, will come together to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is being used in business today, the impact it has achieved and a preview of future AI investment.

“The MSO Symposium serves as a critical platform for industry leaders to examine these evolving dynamics, gain insight from industry leading experts, and explore the innovations that will define the future of collision repair,” said Dan Risley, longstanding conference moderator of the MSO Symposium and senior vice president of sales and development for CCC Intelligent Solutions.

The symposium’s final panel, “The Four Aces”, brings together the CEOs of Boyd Group, Caliber, Classic Collision and Crash Champions. These leaders will share insight into the critical decisions they’re facing in this next era of growth. This candid conversation will explore acquisition and expansion strategies, labor and capacity challenges, AI, capital deployment and more.

“The collision repair landscape is evolving at an unprecedented pace, driven by technological transformation, workforce shifts and changing market dynamics,” said Brian Kaner, CEO of Boyd Group Services and emcee of the 2025 MSO Symposium. “I’m honored to return to the MSO Symposium to join this critical conversation. Given the industry shifts over the past year, bringing leaders together to chart our path forward has never been more vital.”

On Wednesday, Sept. 30, two refurbished vehicles were presented to two San Antonio veterans in need. The donations were made possible by the National Auto Body Council (NABC) Recycled Rides program, vehicle donor GEICO and repair partners Caliber Collision and Crash Champions, and were sponsored by the Collision Industry Electronic Commerce Association (CIECA).

The presentation took place as part of the three-day CIECA CONNEX Conference at the Hilton San Antonio Palacio del Rio. Each year, CIECA CONNEX hosts a NABC Recycled Rides® gifting as part of its annual event, to give back to the community in which the conference is held.

The annual CIECA CONNEX Conference is a forum where industry experts and thought leaders discuss emerging automotive technologies, data exchange, software-defined vehicles and how repairers, insurers, OEMs and other industry stakeholders can keep pace with an ever-changing business environment.
The presentation was kicked off with the presentation of the U.S. colors by the San Antonio Fire Fighters Honor Guard and the Pledge of Allegiance.
A 2020 Toyota CHR, donated by GEICO and refurbished by the technicians at Caliber New Braunfels, was presented to U.S. Army veteran Paula Peterson, who was nominated by Grace After Fire.

“This vehicle will make a huge difference, the first thing I want to do is find a job,” said Peterson. “Making it to my appointments was a struggle. But God always comes through, and all I can say is thank you to everyone that made this happen.”

Peterson is a U.S. Army veteran and single mother who has spent her life fighting, not only for the United States but for the future and safety of her two boys. She immigrated to the U.S. as a child and learned early that survival required strength. Peterson grew up without stability and became self-reliant by the age of six. Despite these beginnings, she worked hard, served proudly as a combat medic and believed deeply in the promise of service, belonging and purpose. Unfortunately, her military career came with life-altering injuries and trauma that have made it difficult to maintain steady employment. Peterson continues working with organizations and service providers to explore part-time opportunities that fit within her physical limitations so she can help put food on the table for her children. Her children also have medical needs along with her father, which has stretched every resource imaginable and exhausted every option for her. This refurbished vehicle from Recycled Rides will give Peterson the ability to regain her independence, earning income through deliveries, accessing food banks, getting to medical appointments and managing her children’s needs safely.
A 2020 Mazda CX-5, donated by GEICO and refurbished by the technicians at Crash Champions, was presented to U.S. Army veteran Casey Franklin, who was nominated by HUD-VASH.

“This vehicle means everything to me, it’s such a beautiful blessing,” said Franklin. “This will elevate life for me and my children, and I just can’t wait to show it to our whole family. I want to share all this information with other veterans … so hopefully you’ll see me again with another veteran receiving this blessing.”

Franklin is a U.S. Army veteran and mother of three, who recently moved to Texas to provide a better life for family. She joined the Army at age 18 and served for 12 years. Since the moment Franklin enrolled in the HUD-VASH program, she has demonstrated patience, resiliency, kindness and professionalism. She is currently pursuing a bachelor’s degree in business and is close to graduating. Franklin strives to do right by her children, and receiving this refurbished vehicle through the NABC Recycled Rides program will provide her the hand up she needs to continue to move forward and provide the best possible life for herself and her family.

Those in the community can support this life-changing program in two ways — donate to the program directly or donate their unwanted or non-running vehicle through the Changing and Saving Lives Keys for Change program. They will receive a tax donation for their contribution, and proceeds will help provide reliable transportation for those in need across the country — and in their community.

Additional partners in this presentation included: ATE; IPAC; Dents and Dings; Sun Auto Tire and Service; Unique Auto Steam Detail; Nexus Towing; Advanced Remarketing Services; Cars for Charity; Copart; and Enterprise.
GEICO, a level one partner of the NABC, has donated more than 1,000 vehicles to people and organizations through Recycled Rides, making it the largest car donor partner of the program.

Caliber Collision, also a level one partner, has refurbished more than 600 vehicles for military service members, veterans and other individuals in need of reliable transportation over the last 12 years.
Crash Champions, also a level one partner of the NABC, has refurbished nearly 300 vehicles for deserving individuals and organizations through Recycled Rides.
